title: Coordinate-divisor criterion for purity of a monomial trait model
statement:
For a prime $\ell$ and $A=\mathbf F_\ell$, use ordinary small-etale derived categories and Tate twists [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories, def-asd-finite-etale-tate-twist]. If $W$ is a regular Noetherian scheme with $\ell$ invertible [def-weil-regular-scheme], say that $W$ is punctually pure at $w\in W$ when, for $W_w=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{W,w}$, $d_w=\dim\mathcal O_{W,w}$ and its closed-point inclusion $j_w:\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(w)\hookrightarrow W_w$, the Kummer fundamental-class map
$$A_{\kappa(w)}\longrightarrow j_w^!A_{W_w}(d_w)[2d_w]$$
of [lem-per-regular-immersion-class-calculus] is an isomorphism. Say that $W$ is punctually pure when this holds at every point. Local rings and residue fields are as in [def-weil-residue-field], affine spectra as in [def-weil-affine-spectrum], and dimension as in [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring].

A trait is $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$ with $R$ a Noetherian local domain of dimension one and principal maximal ideal; a uniformizer $\pi$ generates that maximal ideal. Let $\ell$ be invertible in $R$, let $n\geq1$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbf N$ be not all zero. Put
$$V=\operatorname{Spec}R[T_1,\ldots,T_n]/(\prod_iT_i^{a_i}-\pi).$$
Suppose $V$ is regular. For $a_i>0$ let $h_i:H_i\hookrightarrow V$ be the regular effective Cartier divisor cut out by $T_i=0$ [def-weil-closed-immersion]; effective Cartier means locally defined by a nonzerodivisor. Then $V$ is punctually pure if and only if every supported Kummer map
$$A_{H_i}\longrightarrow h_i^!A_V(1)[2]$$
is an isomorphism. No condition is imposed for indices with $a_i=0$.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(iv), printed p.251; Definitions 3.2.1--3.2.2.

proof.text: Write $B=R[T_1,\ldots,T_n]/(\prod_iT_i^{a_i}-\pi)$, $k=R/(\pi)$ and $U=D_V(\pi)$. The affine scheme $S$ is Noetherian by the assumed Noetherianity of $R$. The images of the finitely many variables generate $B$ over $R$, so $V\to S$ is finite type by [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Thus $V$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian]. Its open subscheme $U$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-open-subscheme-noetherian]. It is regular by [def-weil-regular-scheme], since its local rings are the same as those of $V$. The coefficient prime is invertible on all these schemes because it is already a unit in $R$.

source.place: XVI Lemma 3.5.13(iv), proof, printed p.251; Noetherian hypotheses made explicit

proof.text: For $a_i>0$, setting $T_i=0$ sends the defining monomial to zero, hence sends the relation to $-\pi$. Substitution therefore gives inverse ring homomorphisms $$B/(T_i)\simeq k[T_1,\ldots,\widehat{T_i},\ldots,T_n],$$ taking every remaining variable to itself and each coefficient of $R$ to its residue class. In particular $H_i=\mathbf A_k^{n-1}$. Its structure morphism is finite type by [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], so $H_i$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian], since the spectrum of the field $k$ is Noetherian. It is smooth over $k$ by [sbc-lem-affine-space-smooth] and regular by the smooth-over-regular assertion of [lem-per-regular-lci-geometric-calculus]; a field is regular because its unique local ring has dimension zero and maximal ideal zero. The inclusion $h_i$ has codimension one: the effective Cartier hypothesis says that its ideal is locally generated by the one-element regular sequence $(T_i)$, and codimension is its length, as in [lem-per-regular-lci-geometric-calculus].

source.place: XVI Lemma 3.5.13(iv), proof: the positive-exponent divisors are affine spaces over the residue field, printed p.251

proof.text: Each $H_i$ with $a_i>0$ is punctually pure by [lem-per-prime-field-punctual-purity]: the field $k$ contains its prime field, either $\mathbf Q$ or $\mathbf F_p$, and $H_i$ is a regular Noetherian scheme over that prime field by Step 2. There is no finite-type-over-the-prime-field requirement in the cited statement. The same argument applies to $U=\operatorname{Spec}B[1/\pi]$. The nonzero ring $R[1/\pi]$ is a field: its primes correspond to primes of $R$ not containing $\pi$; the maximal ideal $(\pi)$ is excluded and any nonzero prime strictly below it would give the chain $(0)\subsetneq\mathfrak p\subsetneq(\pi)$, contradicting $\dim R=1$. Hence the only prime of the domain $R[1/\pi]$ is zero, so every nonzero element is a unit. Consequently $U$ is a scheme over a field and hence over a prime field. Step 1 supplies its regularity and Noetherianity, so the cited theorem proves punctual purity of $U$. For $u\in U$, its local ring and closed-point inclusion are exactly those used for $V$ at $u$, so this proves punctual purity of $V$ at every point of $U$. This argument does not require the generic fibre to be smooth over the original fraction field.

source.place: XVI Lemma 3.5.13(iv), proof, printed p.251, using the prime-field purity of Proposition 3.2.5 for the two field-scheme pieces

proof.text: The supports of the positive-exponent $H_i$ cover the special fibre set-theoretically. Indeed a prime ideal $\mathfrak q$ of $B$ contains $\pi$ exactly when it contains $\prod_iT_i^{a_i}$; primality and finiteness of the product imply that this is equivalent to $T_i\in\mathfrak q$ for at least one index with $a_i>0$. Conversely such a $T_i$ forces the product, hence $\pi$, into $\mathfrak q$. Thus every point of $V$ belongs either to $U$ or to some $H_i$ with $a_i>0$. Only supports are asserted to cover: the special fibre need not be reduced, and an index of exponent zero makes no contribution to this argument.

source.place: XVI Lemma 3.5.13(iv), proof: coverage of the special fibre, printed p.251

proof.text: Suppose $V$ is punctually pure. For every $a_i>0$, apply [lem-per-punctual-purity-two-of-three] to the closed pair $h_i:H_i\hookrightarrow V$. The regular Noetherian hypotheses, coefficient invertibility and codimension one were checked in Steps 1--2. Condition (b) of the cited statement holds by Step 3, and condition (c) follows from the present hypothesis on $V$. Its implication (b),(c)$\Rightarrow$(a) gives exactly $$A_{H_i}\xrightarrow{\sim}h_i^!A_V(1)[2].$$ These are the same supported Kummer classes, not merely arbitrary isomorphisms between the objects: both the item and the cited criterion use [lem-per-regular-immersion-class-calculus] as their normalization.

source.place: XVI Lemma 3.5.13(iv), proof, printed p.251, applying Proposition 3.2.3

proof.text: Conversely suppose every displayed positive-exponent divisor map is an isomorphism. In the same application of [lem-per-punctual-purity-two-of-three], condition (a) is now the hypothesis and condition (b) holds by Step 3. Its implication (a),(b)$\Rightarrow$(c) proves punctual purity of $V$ at every point of $H_i$. Step 3 already proves it on $U$, and Step 4 covers every remaining point by some such $H_i$. Thus the defining closed-point Kummer map is invertible at every point of $V$. This proves the converse and the equivalence. For $n=1$ the divisor is $\operatorname{Spec}k$ and the same reasoning applies; zero exponents remain free variables in Step 2 and are never required as boundary components.

source.place: XVI Lemma 3.5.13(iv), proof, printed p.251, applying Proposition 3.2.3

proof_origin.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(iv), proof, printed p.251, using Proposition 3.2.3 and Proposition 3.2.5. The existing prime-field theorem is applied directly to the regular generic open, avoiding an unnecessary generic-smoothness assertion.

Source check: it matches ILO XVI Lemme 3.5.13(iv), printed p.251, whose proof uses affine-space divisors, the special-fibre cover, the generic fibre and Prop 3.2.3. The steps: (1) V and U=D(pi) are Noetherian and regular. (2) B/(T_i)=k[T_j, j≠i] by explicit inverse maps because a_i>0, so H_i is smooth hence regular, with codimension 1; T_i is a nonzerodivisor since (pi,T_i) has height 2 in R[T]. (3) The prime-field purity node applies to H_i and to U, because R[1/pi]=Frac R by the dim-1 chain argument; this avoids needing an exponent invertible in the generic field. (4) The prime cover of the special fibre by the positive-exponent H_i is correct. (5) and (6) use both directions of the two-of-three criterion (ILO 3.2.3) with c=1, and the normalization is the same as the class-calculus Kummer class. Edge cases n=1, (1,0,...,0), and exponents divisible by p or ell work. No duplicate: the semistable, primitive-geometry and 3.5.5 nodes differ. The closures of the cited nodes do not contain the item, and the proof does not use 3.5.6, so there is no monomial-node cycle.
